# Cell Architecture Studio

> Local-first, accessible 3D cell biology and neuroanatomy gallery with 12 schematic specimens, 90 structures mapped to schematic geometry, 164 cited draft facts across 44 sources, and 2D membrane and action-potential simulators.

Registry version: 0.1.0. Totals: 12 specimens, mesh-to-structure mapping complete (90/90 schematic parts linked), 164 cited draft facts, 44 sources, 1,041 procedural mesh instances, ~329,534 estimated triangles. Status: draft teaching content (12/12 biology reviews in draft; not medical advice). Content license: CC BY 4.0; code license: MIT.

## Interactive Views & Simulators

- **Explore (`/`)**: Browse all 12 specimens, inspect structures, read cited facts, and control the 3D scene.
- **Compare (`/compare`)**: Compare any two specimens side by side with two isolated 3D scene graphs, shared structure focus, and a 6-trait table.
- **Learn (`/learn`)**: Offline flashcards, 4-option quizzes, cited static Ask helper, and local IndexedDB v2 progress with export/delete.
- **Lab (`/lab`)**: Two 2D HTML5 canvas simulations that run without WebGL — Phospholipid bilayer self-assembly (313 molecules) and Action potential (voltage-gated Na+/K+ channels and myelinated saltatory conduction).
- **About (`/about`)**: Biology review status, CC BY 4.0 provenance, full source list, accessibility statement, and local privacy controls.

## Camera & Annotation Controls

- **OrbitControls**: Pointer drag orbit with damping (pan disabled, polar clamp 0.12π–0.88π, zoom distance 1.05–8.5).
- **Mesh / Focus**: Switch between full-specimen framing (`Mesh`) and bounding-box camera framing (`Focus`) on the selected structure via `CameraDirector`.
- **Cutaway**: Hides outer shell parts marked `cutawayHide` to reveal internal organelles or subcortical tracts.
- **Auto-rotate / Reset view / Save PNG**: Toggle gentle rotation (disabled when `prefers-reduced-motion` is enabled, paused on drag or hidden tab), reset camera to canonical framing, or export a PNG snapshot.
- **Raycast Picking & Keyboard List**: `PointerPicker` clicks in 3D synchronize two-way with the keyboard-accessible structure list and cited detail inspector (including schematic mesh-to-structure mapping, biology review status, schematic notes, and a local copyable correction report).

## 3D Rendering Details

- **Engine**: Imperative Three.js (`@cas/viewer-core`) in a lazy-loaded chunk using `WebGLRenderer` (antialias, alpha, `preserveDrawingBuffer: true`, `SRGBColorSpace`, `ACESFilmicToneMapping` exposure `1.05`, pixel ratio <= 2) and `PerspectiveCamera` (38° FOV).
- **Lighting**: `PMREMGenerator` + `RoomEnvironment` IBL plus hemisphere, warm key, cool rim, and soft fill directional lights over a translucent circular stage.
- **Geometry**: 100% repository-authored procedural schematic geometry (27 primitives + deterministic seeded repeat patterns `scatter`, `shell`, `ring`, `line`, `helix`, `grid`). Every structural mesh carries an authored `structureId`. Previews (`/previews/*.svg`) are rendered deterministically from the same expanded instances.

## Specimens & Structures

### Plant cell (Elodea sp.)

- **Domain / Cell type**: plant · Mesophyll cell
- **Size & scale**: Typically tens of micrometres across — All geometry is schematic and unitless. No real-world scale is inferred from the model; the size note is a separate textbook range.
- **3D stats**: 77 mesh instances · ~20,344 estimated triangles · Capabilities: 3D procedural mesh, Structure camera focus, Cutaway shell toggle, Mesh-mapped highlighting, PNG screenshot export, GLB export capability · Preview: `/previews/plant-cell.svg`
- **Summary**: A photosynthetic plant cell: cellulose wall, large central vacuole, and chloroplasts pressed against the periphery.
- **Overview**: This schematic shows a mesophyll cell, the photosynthetic tissue inside a leaf. Unlike an animal cell, it is enclosed by a cellulose cell wall and usually dominated by a large central vacuole. Chloroplasts sit near the plasma membrane, where light and CO₂ are available. The model is illustrative: it does not represent cell size, organelle counts, or membrane ultrastructure to scale.
- **Traits**: Nucleus: Present | Cell wall: Cellulose primary wall | Chloroplasts: Present | Motility: Sessile; no cell crawling | Typical size: Tens of µm | Organisation: Eukaryotic, multicellular tissue
- **Structures (7)**:
  - **Cell wall** (mesh-to-structure mapping complete; meshes: cell-wall, plasmodesma-0..5 (6)): A rigid extracellular layer composed primarily of cellulose outside the plasma membrane. Function: Maintains cell shape, protects the cell, and resists turgor pressure so the cell does not take up water without limit.
    - Fact: Plant cell walls have cellulose—a polysaccharide made of glucose units—as their major organic molecule. [OpenStax, §4.3, 'The Cell Wall' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/4-3-eukaryotic-cells)]
    - Fact: The cell wall is a rigid covering external to the plasma membrane that protects the cell, provides structural support, and gives it shape. [OpenStax, §4.3, 'The Cell Wall' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/4-3-eukaryotic-cells)]
  - **Plasma membrane** (mesh-to-structure mapping complete; meshes: plasma-membrane): A phospholipid bilayer with embedded proteins that sits just inside the cell wall and controls exchange with the environment. Function: Selectively regulates the movement of ions, water, and small molecules into and out of the cell.
    - Fact: The plasma membrane is a phospholipid bilayer with embedded proteins that controls the passage of organic molecules, ions, water, and oxygen into and out of the cell. [OpenStax, §4.3, 'The Plasma Membrane' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/4-3-eukaryotic-cells)]
    - Fact: In plant cells, the rigid cell wall sits external to the plasma membrane. [OpenStax, §4.3, 'The Cell Wall' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/4-3-eukaryotic-cells)]
  - **Central vacuole** (mesh-to-structure mapping complete; meshes: central-vacuole): A large membrane-bound compartment that can occupy most of a mature plant cell's volume. Function: Stores water, ions, nutrients, and sometimes pigments or defensive compounds; its turgor pressure helps support the cell.
    - Fact: A plant cell's large central vacuole occupies most of the cell's volume and helps regulate cellular water concentration in changing conditions. [OpenStax, §4.3, 'The Central Vacuole' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/4-3-eukaryotic-cells)]
  - **Nucleus** (mesh-to-structure mapping complete; meshes: nucleus, nucleus-chromatin, nucleolus, nuclear-pore): The DNA-containing organelle, bounded by a double membrane and containing a dense nucleolus. Function: Stores most of the cell's genetic material and coordinates gene expression, growth, and division.
    - Fact: The nucleus is bounded by a nuclear envelope punctuated with pores and houses the cell's DNA. [OpenStax, §4.3, 'The Nucleus' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/4-3-eukaryotic-cells)]
    - Fact: The nucleolus is the site of ribosomal RNA synthesis and ribosomal subunit assembly. [OpenStax, §4.3, 'The Nucleolus' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/4-3-eukaryotic-cells)]
  - **Chloroplast** (mesh-to-structure mapping complete; meshes: chloroplast-0..7 (8), chloroplast-granum-a-0..7 (8), chloroplast-granum-b-0..7 (8), chloroplast-lamella-0..7 (8)): A double-membrane plastid containing chlorophyll and stacked thylakoid membranes. Function: Captures light energy and converts it into chemical energy during photosynthesis, releasing oxygen from water.
    - Fact: Chloroplasts carry out photosynthesis using chlorophyll and internal thylakoid membrane stacks called grana. [OpenStax, §4.3, 'Chloroplasts' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/4-3-eukaryotic-cells)]
    - Fact: Chloroplasts have an outer and inner membrane and carry their own genome on a single circular chromosome. [OpenStax, §4.3, 'Chloroplasts' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/4-3-eukaryotic-cells)]
  - **Mitochondrion** (mesh-to-structure mapping complete; meshes: mitochondrion-0..4 (5), mitochondrion-cristae-0..4 (5)): A double-membrane organelle whose inner membrane is folded into cristae. Function: Produces ATP through aerobic respiration and participates in other metabolic pathways.
    - Fact: Mitochondria produce ATP by aerobic respiration, and their inner membrane is folded into cristae. [OpenStax, §4.3, 'Mitochondria' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/4-3-eukaryotic-cells)]
    - Fact: Mitochondria contain their own circular DNA and ribosomes and divide independently by a process resembling prokaryotic binary fission. [OpenStax, §23.1, 'Mitochondria' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/23-1-eukaryotic-origins)]
  - **Golgi apparatus** (mesh-to-structure mapping complete; meshes: golgi, golgi-vesicle): A stack of flattened membrane sacs that modifies and sorts proteins and lipids. Function: Receives cargo from the endoplasmic reticulum, modifies it, and packages it into vesicles for delivery.
    - Fact: The Golgi apparatus modifies, sorts, packages, and distributes lipids and proteins into vesicles. [OpenStax, §4.4, 'The Golgi Apparatus' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/4-4-the-endomembrane-system-and-proteins)]
    - Fact: Golgi cisternae form a series of flattened membranous sacs with a receiving cis face and an outgoing trans face. [OpenStax, §4.4, 'The Golgi Apparatus' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/4-4-the-endomembrane-system-and-proteins)]

### White blood cell (Homo sapiens)

- **Domain / Cell type**: animal · Neutrophil (segmented granulocyte)
- **Size & scale**: Roughly 9–15 µm diameter — Schematic and unitless. The pseudopods and granules are enlarged for legibility; no real-world scale is encoded.
- **3D stats**: 78 mesh instances · ~19,280 estimated triangles · Capabilities: 3D procedural mesh, Structure camera focus, Cutaway shell toggle, Mesh-mapped highlighting, PNG screenshot export, GLB export capability · Preview: `/previews/white-blood-cell.svg`
- **Summary**: A motile immune cell with a multi-lobed nucleus, enzyme-rich granules, and actin-driven pseudopods.
- **Overview**: Neutrophils patrol blood and tissue, following chemical cues to sites of infection. They are specialised for rapid response: a lobed nucleus, abundant granules, and a flexible actin cytoskeleton let them squeeze through tissue and engulf microbes. This schematic emphasises those features; granule counts and nuclear lobe shape vary between real cells.
- **Traits**: Nucleus: Present, multi-lobed | Cell wall: Absent | Chloroplasts: Absent | Motility: Amoeboid; chemotaxis | Typical size: 9–15 µm | Organisation: Eukaryotic, single cell in blood/tissue
- **Structures (6)**:
  - **Plasma membrane** (mesh-to-structure mapping complete; meshes: plasma-membrane): The selectively permeable outer membrane of the neutrophil, specialised for sensing, adhesion, and engulfment. Function: Controls exchange, carries chemotactic receptors, and rearranges to form a phagosome around a target.
    - Fact: Neutrophils move through tissue spaces like amoebas, extending their plasma membranes toward chemical signals (positive chemotaxis). [OpenStax, §18.4, 'Leukocytes' (https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/18-4-leukocytes-and-platelets)]
    - Fact: During phagocytosis a leukocyte's plasma membrane invaginates around a pathogen and pinches off to form an internal vesicle. [OpenStax, §4.4, 'Lysosomes' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/4-4-the-endomembrane-system-and-proteins)]
  - **Multi-lobed nucleus** (mesh-to-structure mapping complete; meshes: nucleus-lobe-0..3 (4), nucleus-bridge-0..2 (3)): A nucleus divided into several connected lobes, characteristic of mature segmented neutrophils. Function: Houses the cell's DNA; the lobed shape is associated with the mature, circulating form of the cell.
    - Fact: Mature neutrophils typically have a nucleus with two to five lobes. [OpenStax, §18.4, 'Leukocytes' (https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/18-4-leukocytes-and-platelets)]
    - Fact: Neutrophils are classified as granular leukocytes because of their lobed nucleus and cytoplasmic granules. [OpenStax, §18.4, 'Leukocytes' (https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/18-4-leukocytes-and-platelets)]
  - **Cytoplasmic granules** (mesh-to-structure mapping complete; meshes: granules-primary, granules-secondary): Membrane-bound storage vesicles containing enzymes and antimicrobial compounds. Function: Release their contents into a phagosome or the extracellular space to kill and digest microbes.
    - Fact: Neutrophils release chemicals from their cytoplasmic granules to destroy pathogens. [OpenStax, §18.4, 'Leukocytes' (https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/18-4-leukocytes-and-platelets)]
    - Fact: Granulocytes contain abundant cytoplasmic granules that stain distinctly depending on the cell type. [OpenStax, §18.4, 'Leukocytes' (https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/18-4-leukocytes-and-platelets)]
  - **Mitochondrion** (mesh-to-structure mapping complete; meshes: mitochondrion-0, mitochondrion-1, mitochondrion-cristae-0, mitochondrion-cristae-1): Sparse double-membrane organelles that regulate chemotaxis, reactive oxygen signalling, and survival while glycolysis supplies most ATP. Function: Mature neutrophils rely primarily on glycolysis for ATP and NADPH oxidase (NOX2) for the respiratory burst, while mitochondria modulate leading-edge purinergic chemotaxis, mROS signalling, NETosis, and apoptosis.
    - Fact: Mature neutrophils rely mainly on glycolysis for ATP production, while mitochondria regulate chemotactic migration, mitochondrial ROS signalling, NET formation, and survival. [Europe PMC / Frontiers, Abstract & 'Migration and adhesion' (https://europepmc.org/article/MED/36081497)]
    - Fact: The neutrophil respiratory burst is driven primarily by NADPH oxidase (NOX2), with mitochondrial ROS and fatty acid metabolism modulating NADPH supply and bactericidal activity. [Europe PMC / Frontiers, 'Respiratory burst' (https://europepmc.org/article/MED/36081497)]
  - **Pseudopod** (mesh-to-structure mapping complete; meshes: pseudopod-0..3 (4)): A temporary cytoplasmic extension produced by actin polymerisation at the leading edge. Function: Drives amoeboid crawling toward chemical signals and reaches around particles during phagocytosis.
    - Fact: Neutrophils move through tissue spaces like amoebas by extending their plasma membranes toward chemical signals. [OpenStax, §18.4, 'Leukocytes' (https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/18-4-leukocytes-and-platelets)]
    - Fact: Actin microfilaments can depolymerize and reform rapidly to enable changes in cell shape and movement. [OpenStax, §4.5, 'Microfilaments' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/4-5-the-cytoskeleton)]
  - **Actin cytoskeleton** (mesh-to-structure mapping complete; meshes: actin-filament-0..9 (10)): A dynamic network of actin filaments that supports shape change and force generation. Function: Powers crawling, membrane ruffling, and the contractile ring used to internalise a phagosome.
    - Fact: Microfilaments are built from two intertwined actin strands that assemble with ATP and disassemble quickly to drive movement. [OpenStax, §4.5, 'Microfilaments' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/4-5-the-cytoskeleton)]

### Neuron (Mammalian (schematic))

- **Domain / Cell type**: animal · Multipolar motor neuron
- **Size & scale**: Soma 10–30 µm; axon may extend up to about a metre in humans — Schematic and unitless. Axon length is compressed; the model cannot be used to estimate real dimensions.
- **3D stats**: 85 mesh instances · ~25,476 estimated triangles · Capabilities: 3D procedural mesh, Structure camera focus, Cutaway shell toggle, Mesh-mapped highlighting, PNG screenshot export, GLB export capability · Preview: `/previews/neuron.svg`
- **Summary**: A signal-conducting cell with a receptive soma and dendrites, a long axon, insulating myelin, and transmitter-releasing terminals.
- **Overview**: Neurons are polarised cells built for communication. Dendrites collect inputs, the soma integrates them, and the axon carries an action potential to terminals that release neurotransmitter onto the next cell. The myelin sheath shown here is a schematic of the insulating wrapping provided by glial cells. Real neurons vary enormously in shape, and many have thousands of synaptic contacts not depicted here.
- **Traits**: Nucleus: Present | Cell wall: Absent | Chloroplasts: Absent | Motility: No crawling; conducts electrical signals | Typical size: Soma 10–30 µm; axon up to ~1 m | Organisation: Eukaryotic, nervous tissue
- **Structures (7)**:
  - **Soma (cell body)** (mesh-to-structure mapping complete; meshes: soma, axon-hillock, soma-nissl-0..2 (3)): The compact cell body containing the nucleus and most biosynthetic machinery. Function: Integrates incoming signals and maintains the cell's metabolism; it is the origin of the axon.
    - Fact: The neuronal cell body, or soma, contains the nucleus and most of the cell's organelles. [OpenStax, §35.1, 'Neurons' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/35-1-neurons-and-glial-cells)]
    - Fact: In a multipolar neuron, dendrites and a single axon extend from the cell body. [OpenStax, §35.1, 'Neurons' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/35-1-neurons-and-glial-cells)]
  - **Nucleus** (mesh-to-structure mapping complete; meshes: nucleus, nucleus-chromatin, nucleolus, nuclear-pore): The neuron's DNA-containing organelle, housed within the cell body alongside biosynthetic machinery. Function: Directs protein synthesis needed for neurotransmission, plasticity, and cell maintenance.
    - Fact: The neuronal soma contains a nucleus that stores the cell's genetic material along with major organelles. [OpenStax, §35.1, 'Neurons' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/35-1-neurons-and-glial-cells)]
  - **Dendrites** (mesh-to-structure mapping complete; meshes: dendrite-trunk-0..5 (6), dendrite-branch-0..9 (10), dendrite-spine-0..9 (10)): Branching processes that receive synaptic inputs and carry graded signals toward the soma. Function: Increase the receptive surface area and integrate inputs from other neurons.
    - Fact: Dendrites are branched processes that receive synaptic signals and usually generate graded potentials toward the cell body. [OpenStax, §12.5, 'Graded Potentials' (https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/12-5-communication-between-neurons)]
    - Fact: Dendrites can carry small protrusions called dendritic spines that increase surface area for synaptic connections. [OpenStax, §35.1, 'Neurons' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/35-1-neurons-and-glial-cells)]
  - **Axon** (mesh-to-structure mapping complete; meshes: axon, axon-node-0..3 (4)): A single long process that conducts action potentials away from the soma toward axon terminals. Function: Transmits electrical signals over distance without decrement, thanks to voltage-gated ion channels.
    - Fact: The axon is a process that carries signals away from the cell body toward target cells. [OpenStax, §35.1, 'Neurons' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/35-1-neurons-and-glial-cells)]
    - Fact: Action potentials are regenerated along the axon by voltage-gated Na+ and K+ channels rather than decaying with distance. [OpenStax, §35.2, 'How Neurons Communicate' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/35-2-how-neurons-communicate)]
  - **Myelin sheath** (mesh-to-structure mapping complete; meshes: myelin-sheath-0..4 (5), myelin-core-0..4 (5)): A multilayered glial wrapping around segments of some axons, interrupted at nodes of Ranvier. Function: Electrically insulates the axon and enables fast saltatory conduction between nodes.
    - Fact: In the peripheral nervous system myelin is produced by Schwann cells; in the central nervous system by oligodendrocytes. [OpenStax, §35.1, 'Glial Cells' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/35-1-neurons-and-glial-cells)]
    - Fact: Myelination increases conduction speed by enabling saltatory conduction as the action potential jumps between nodes of Ranvier. [OpenStax, §12.4, 'Propagation of the Action Potential' (https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/12-4-the-action-potential)]
  - **Axon terminals** (mesh-to-structure mapping complete; meshes: axon-branch-0..3 (4), axon-bouton-0..3 (4), axon-vesicle-a-0..3 (4), axon-vesicle-b-0..3 (4)): Specialised endings where the axon contacts a target cell and releases neurotransmitter. Function: Convert an incoming action potential into chemical signalling across a synapse.
    - Fact: Axon terminals contain synaptic vesicles that release neurotransmitter when calcium enters after an action potential. [OpenStax, §35.2, 'How Neurons Communicate' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/35-2-how-neurons-communicate)]
    - Fact: A synapse is the junction where a presynaptic terminal communicates with a postsynaptic cell. [OpenStax, §35.2, 'How Neurons Communicate' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/35-2-how-neurons-communicate)]
  - **Mitochondrion** (mesh-to-structure mapping complete; meshes: mitochondrion-0..4 (5), mitochondrion-cristae-0..4 (5)): An ATP-generating organelle enriched in regions with high energy demand such as terminals. Function: Supplies ATP for ion pumps, vesicle trafficking, and neurotransmitter recycling.
    - Fact: Mitochondria generate ATP by aerobic respiration inside eukaryotic cells, including neurons. [OpenStax, §4.3, 'Mitochondria' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/4-3-eukaryotic-cells)]
    - Fact: Ongoing Na+/K+ pump activity requires ATP and helps return the neuronal membrane to its resting potential. [OpenStax, §12.4, 'The Action Potential' (https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/12-4-the-action-potential)]

### Epithelial cell (Homo sapiens)

- **Domain / Cell type**: animal · Intestinal enterocyte
- **Size & scale**: Roughly 10 µm wide and 20 µm tall — Schematic and unitless. Microvillus density and membrane thickness are exaggerated for legibility.
- **3D stats**: 137 mesh instances · ~38,256 estimated triangles · Capabilities: 3D procedural mesh, Structure camera focus, Cutaway shell toggle, Mesh-mapped highlighting, PNG screenshot export, GLB export capability · Preview: `/previews/epithelial-cell.svg`
- **Summary**: A polarised absorptive cell: a dense apical brush border, a sealing tight junction, and energy-hungry basolateral transport.
- **Overview**: Enterocytes line the small intestine and absorb nutrients. Their apical surface carries a dense brush border of microvilli, while their basolateral surface contacts neighbouring cells and the basement membrane. Tight junctions separate these domains and limit leakage between cells. This schematic highlights that polarity rather than the full cytoskeletal and membrane architecture.
- **Traits**: Nucleus: Present | Cell wall: Absent | Chloroplasts: Absent | Motility: Anchored; polarised sheet | Typical size: ~10 µm wide, 20 µm tall | Organisation: Eukaryotic, epithelial sheet
- **Structures (7)**:
  - **Apical brush border** (mesh-to-structure mapping complete; meshes: apical-membrane, microvillus): A dense array of actin-supported microvilli on the apical membrane, forming the brush border. Function: Multiplies the apical surface area for nutrient and ion absorption.
    - Fact: Microvilli are cylindrical apical surface extensions of the intestinal epithelial plasma membrane that increase the surface area available for absorption. [OpenStax, §23.5, 'Microvilli' (https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/23-5-the-small-and-large-intestines)]
  - **Tight junction** (mesh-to-structure mapping complete; meshes: tight-junction, tight-junction-lower): A belt-like junction near the apical surface that seals the space between adjacent epithelial cells. Function: Limits paracellular leakage and helps separate apical from basolateral membrane domains.
    - Fact: Tight junctions eliminate extracellular space between adjacent epithelial cells and block movement of substances between the cells. [OpenStax, §4.2, 'Cell-to-Cell Junctions' (https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/4-2-epithelial-tissue)]
    - Fact: Tight junctions separate epithelial cells into distinct apical and basal compartments. [OpenStax, §4.2, 'Cell-to-Cell Junctions' (https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/4-2-epithelial-tissue)]
  - **Basolateral membrane** (mesh-to-structure mapping complete; meshes: basolateral-shell, basolateral-contact, desmosome-0..5 (6)): The side and basal surfaces of the cell that contact neighbouring cells and the basement membrane. Function: Carries transporters that move absorbed nutrients into the blood and maintain ion gradients.
    - Fact: Epithelial cells exhibit a polarized distribution of organelles and membrane-bound proteins between their apical and basal surfaces. [OpenStax, §4.2, 'Epithelial Tissue' (https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/4-2-epithelial-tissue)]
    - Fact: The basal surface attaches to a basal lamina and reticular lamina forming a basement membrane above underlying connective tissue. [OpenStax, §4.2, 'Epithelial Tissue' (https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/4-2-epithelial-tissue)]
  - **Nucleus** (mesh-to-structure mapping complete; meshes: nucleus, nucleus-chromatin, nucleolus, nuclear-pore): The DNA-containing organelle, positioned toward the basal side of this polarised cell. Function: Controls protein synthesis, including the transporters and enzymes needed for absorption.
    - Fact: The nucleus houses the cell's DNA and directs the synthesis of ribosomes and proteins. [OpenStax, §4.3, 'The Nucleus' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/4-3-eukaryotic-cells)]
    - Fact: In simple columnar epithelial cells the nucleus tends to be elongated and located toward the basal end. [OpenStax, §4.2, 'Classification of Epithelial Tissues' (https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/4-2-epithelial-tissue)]
  - **Mitochondrion** (mesh-to-structure mapping complete; meshes: mitochondrion-0..5 (6), mitochondrion-cristae-0..5 (6)): An ATP-producing organelle abundant in absorptive epithelial cells. Function: Powers active transport across the apical and basolateral membranes.
    - Fact: Mitochondria produce ATP by aerobic respiration, and their inner membrane is folded into cristae. [OpenStax, §4.3, 'Mitochondria' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/4-3-eukaryotic-cells)]
    - Fact: Moving substances against concentration gradients via active transport requires cellular energy, usually in the form of ATP. [OpenStax, §5.3, 'Active Transport' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/5-3-active-transport)]
  - **Rough endoplasmic reticulum** (mesh-to-structure mapping complete; meshes: rough-er-sheet, rough-er-ribosome): A network of ribosome-studded membrane sheets specialised for protein synthesis. Function: Produces membrane proteins, secreted enzymes, and transporters for the cell's absorptive role.
    - Fact: Rough endoplasmic reticulum is studded with ribosomes and is a major site of protein synthesis. [OpenStax, §4.4, 'The Endoplasmic Reticulum' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/4-4-the-endomembrane-system-and-proteins)]
    - Fact: Ribosomes transfer newly synthesized proteins into the rough ER lumen where they undergo folding or modification before leaving in transport vesicles. [OpenStax, §4.4, 'Rough ER' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/4-4-the-endomembrane-system-and-proteins)]
  - **Golgi apparatus** (mesh-to-structure mapping complete; meshes: golgi, golgi-vesicle): A stack of flattened membrane sacs that modifies, sorts, and packages proteins. Function: Routes newly made membrane and secreted proteins to their correct destinations.
    - Fact: The Golgi apparatus modifies, sorts, and packages proteins and lipids into vesicles. [OpenStax, §4.4, 'The Golgi Apparatus' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/4-4-the-endomembrane-system-and-proteins)]
    - Fact: The Golgi is part of the endomembrane system and receives cargo from the endoplasmic reticulum. [OpenStax, §4.4, 'The Endomembrane System' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/4-4-the-endomembrane-system-and-proteins)]

### Bacterium (Escherichia coli)

- **Domain / Cell type**: bacteria · Gram-negative rod
- **Size & scale**: Roughly 0.5 µm wide and 2 µm long — Schematic and unitless. Ribosome number, pili density, and flagellar length are approximate teaching choices.
- **3D stats**: 93 mesh instances · ~43,656 estimated triangles · Capabilities: 3D procedural mesh, Structure camera focus, Cutaway shell toggle, Mesh-mapped highlighting, PNG screenshot export, GLB export capability · Preview: `/previews/bacteria.svg`
- **Summary**: A prokaryotic cell: no membrane-bound nucleus, a layered envelope, a nucleoid, 70S ribosomes, and a rotary flagellum.
- **Overview**: Bacteria are prokaryotes: their DNA is not enclosed in a membrane-bound nucleus, and they lack the membrane-bound organelles of eukaryotes. This schematic E. coli shows the Gram-negative envelope (outer membrane, peptidoglycan wall, inner membrane), a tangled nucleoid, ribosomes, a helical flagellum, and surface pili. The envelope cutaway is authored so the interior can be inspected without pretending to be a physical slice.
- **Traits**: Nucleus: Absent (nucleoid instead) | Cell wall: Peptidoglycan envelope | Chloroplasts: Absent | Motility: Flagellar swimming | Typical size: ~0.5 × 2 µm | Organisation: Prokaryotic, single cell
- **Structures (7)**:
  - **Outer membrane** (mesh-to-structure mapping complete; meshes: outer-membrane, outer-porin-0..4 (5)): The outermost lipid bilayer of the Gram-negative cell envelope, outside the peptidoglycan layer. Function: Forms a permeability barrier and contains proteins that mediate transport and structural connections.
    - Fact: Gram-negative bacteria have a thin peptidoglycan layer surrounded by a periplasmic space and a second lipid bilayer called the outer membrane. [OpenStax, §3.3, 'Cell Wall' (https://openstax.org/books/microbiology/pages/3-3-unique-characteristics-of-prokaryotic-cells)]
    - Fact: The outer leaflet of the Gram-negative outer membrane contains lipopolysaccharide (LPS). [OpenStax, §3.3, 'Cell Wall' (https://openstax.org/books/microbiology/pages/3-3-unique-characteristics-of-prokaryotic-cells)]
  - **Peptidoglycan cell wall** (mesh-to-structure mapping complete; meshes: cell-wall): A mesh polymer of sugars and short peptides that lies between the two membranes of a Gram-negative rod. Function: Maintains cell shape and resists osmotic pressure; its synthesis is the target of penicillin-type antibiotics.
    - Fact: Bacterial cell walls contain peptidoglycan, a meshwork of alternating NAG and NAM sugars cross-linked by peptides that maintains shape and resists osmotic pressure. [OpenStax, §3.3, 'Cell Wall' (https://openstax.org/books/microbiology/pages/3-3-unique-characteristics-of-prokaryotic-cells)]
    - Fact: Gram-negative bacteria have a comparatively thin peptidoglycan layer (up to about 4 nm thick) beneath their outer membrane. [OpenStax, §3.3, 'Cell Wall' (https://openstax.org/books/microbiology/pages/3-3-unique-characteristics-of-prokaryotic-cells)]
  - **Plasma membrane** (mesh-to-structure mapping complete; meshes: plasma-membrane): The inner lipid bilayer that encloses the bacterial cytoplasm. Function: Regulates transport and hosts many energy-conversion and biosynthetic systems.
    - Fact: Most bacterial plasma membranes are phospholipid bilayers embedded with proteins that form a selectively permeable barrier. [OpenStax, §3.3, 'Plasma Membrane' (https://openstax.org/books/microbiology/pages/3-3-unique-characteristics-of-prokaryotic-cells)]
    - Fact: Prokaryotes lack a nucleus and lack membrane-bound organelles inside their cytoplasm. [OpenStax, §4.2, 'Prokaryotic Cells' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/4-2-prokaryotic-cells)]
  - **Nucleoid** (mesh-to-structure mapping complete; meshes: nucleoid, nucleoid-loop-b, nucleoid-plasmid-a, nucleoid-plasmid-b): The region containing the bacterium's circular chromosome, not enclosed by a membrane. Function: Stores and replicates the genetic material; transcription and translation are coupled in the cytoplasm.
    - Fact: Prokaryotic DNA is found in a nucleoid region that is not surrounded by a membrane. [OpenStax, §4.2, 'Prokaryotic Cells' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/4-2-prokaryotic-cells)]
    - Fact: In prokaryotes, chromosomal DNA is organized into a single circular chromosome. [OpenStax, §4.3, 'Eukaryotic Cells' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/4-3-eukaryotic-cells)]
  - **Ribosome** (mesh-to-structure mapping complete; meshes: ribosome): A ribonucleoprotein machine that translates messenger RNA into protein. Function: Synthesises proteins, using a 70S bacterial ribosome rather than the 80S eukaryotic type.
    - Fact: Prokaryotic ribosomes are 70S particles (30S and 50S subunits), distinct from the 80S cytoplasmic ribosomes of eukaryotes. [OpenStax, §3.3, 'Ribosomes' (https://openstax.org/books/microbiology/pages/3-3-unique-characteristics-of-prokaryotic-cells)]
    - Fact: Ribosomes in the bacterial cytoplasm synthesize proteins by translating mRNA. [OpenStax, §3.3, 'Ribosomes' (https://openstax.org/books/microbiology/pages/3-3-unique-characteristics-of-prokaryotic-cells)]
  - **Flagellum** (mesh-to-structure mapping complete; meshes: flagellum-filament, flagellum-filament-b, flagellum-hook, flagellum-motor-l, flagellum-motor-ms): A long helical filament rotated by a membrane-embedded motor to propel the cell. Function: Drives swimming motility and chemotaxis toward favourable conditions.
    - Fact: A bacterial flagellum consists of a stiff spiral flagellin filament linked by a hook to a membrane-embedded basal body motor. [OpenStax, §3.3, 'Flagella' (https://openstax.org/books/microbiology/pages/3-3-unique-characteristics-of-prokaryotic-cells)]
    - Fact: Bacterial flagella spin in aqueous solution, rotating counterclockwise to run and clockwise to tumble during chemotaxis. [OpenStax, §3.3, 'Flagella' (https://openstax.org/books/microbiology/pages/3-3-unique-characteristics-of-prokaryotic-cells)]
  - **Pili** (mesh-to-structure mapping complete; meshes: pilus-0..23 (24)): Short protein appendages on the bacterial surface, distinct from the flagellum. Function: Mediate attachment to surfaces and, for some pili, horizontal DNA transfer between cells.
    - Fact: Pili and fimbriae are protein appendages on the bacterial surface that help cells attach to surfaces. [OpenStax, §3.3, 'Fimbriae and Pili' (https://openstax.org/books/microbiology/pages/3-3-unique-characteristics-of-prokaryotic-cells)]
    - Fact: Pili exchange genetic material between bacteria through direct contact during conjugation. [OpenStax, §4.2, 'Prokaryotic Cells' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/4-2-prokaryotic-cells)]

### Animal cell (Mammalia (unspecified lineage))

- **Domain / Cell type**: animal · Generic mammalian cell
- **Size & scale**: Commonly 10–30 µm across — Schematic and unitless. Organelle size, number, and position vary by cell type and are not measured.
- **3D stats**: 115 mesh instances · ~26,396 estimated triangles · Capabilities: 3D procedural mesh, Structure camera focus, Cutaway shell toggle, Mesh-mapped highlighting, PNG screenshot export, GLB export capability · Preview: `/previews/animal-cell.svg`
- **Summary**: A generalised eukaryotic animal cell: no wall or chloroplasts, but a nucleus, endomembrane system, mitochondria, and lysosomes.
- **Overview**: This specimen is a reference animal cell rather than a portrait of one particular cell type. It shows features shared by most mammalian cells: a flexible plasma membrane, a nucleus, rough and smooth endoplasmic reticulum, a Golgi apparatus, mitochondria, and lysosomes. Specialised cells add their own structures—muscle sarcomeres, neuronal processes, epithelial junctions—which are represented by the other specimens.
- **Traits**: Nucleus: Present | Cell wall: Absent | Chloroplasts: Absent | Motility: Limited; lineage-dependent | Typical size: 10–30 µm | Organisation: Eukaryotic, animal tissue
- **Structures (7)**:
  - **Plasma membrane** (mesh-to-structure mapping complete; meshes: plasma-membrane): The flexible outer phospholipid bilayer that defines the cell and mediates exchange. Function: Controls transport, receives signals, and anchors the cell to neighbours and the extracellular matrix.
    - Fact: The plasma membrane is a phospholipid bilayer with embedded proteins that regulates transport and signal transmission. [OpenStax, §5.1, 'Fluid Mosaic Model' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/5-1-components-and-structure)]
    - Fact: Animal cells lack a cell wall; secreted proteins and carbohydrates form an extracellular matrix and the cytoskeleton supports cell shape. [OpenStax, §4.6, 'Extracellular Matrix of Animal Cells' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/4-6-connections-between-cells-and-cellular-activities)]
  - **Nucleus** (mesh-to-structure mapping complete; meshes: nucleus, nucleus-chromatin, nucleolus, nuclear-pore): The double-membrane organelle that houses the cell's chromosomal DNA. Function: Stores genetic information and coordinates transcription, growth, and division.
    - Fact: The nucleus is bounded by a nuclear envelope with pores and houses the cell's DNA. [OpenStax, §4.3, 'The Nucleus' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/4-3-eukaryotic-cells)]
    - Fact: The nucleolus aggregates ribosomal RNA with proteins to assemble ribosomal subunits. [OpenStax, §4.3, 'The Nucleolus' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/4-3-eukaryotic-cells)]
  - **Rough endoplasmic reticulum** (mesh-to-structure mapping complete; meshes: rough-er-0..5 (6), rough-er-ribosome): Flattened membrane cisternae studded with ribosomes, continuous with the nuclear envelope. Function: Synthesises and folds membrane and secreted proteins, then routes them toward the Golgi.
    - Fact: Rough endoplasmic reticulum is studded with ribosomes and is a major site of protein synthesis. [OpenStax, §4.4, 'Rough ER' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/4-4-the-endomembrane-system-and-proteins)]
    - Fact: The ER membrane is continuous with the nuclear envelope and sends proteins in transport vesicles to the Golgi. [OpenStax, §4.4, 'The Endoplasmic Reticulum' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/4-4-the-endomembrane-system-and-proteins)]
  - **Smooth endoplasmic reticulum** (mesh-to-structure mapping complete; meshes: smooth-er-0..8 (9)): A tubular ER network lacking ribosomes, specialised for lipid and steroid synthesis and detoxification. Function: Produces lipids, stores calcium, and helps metabolise drugs and toxins in some cell types.
    - Fact: Smooth ER has few or no ribosomes and participates in lipid and steroid hormone synthesis, detoxification, and calcium storage. [OpenStax, §4.4, 'Smooth ER' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/4-4-the-endomembrane-system-and-proteins)]
    - Fact: Cells that synthesize large amounts of steroid hormones, such as those in the ovaries and testes, contain abundant smooth ER. [OpenStax, §3.2, 'Endoplasmic Reticulum' (https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/3-2-the-cytoplasm-and-cellular-organelles)]
  - **Golgi apparatus** (mesh-to-structure mapping complete; meshes: golgi, golgi-vesicle): A stack of flattened membrane cisternae that modifies and sorts proteins and lipids. Function: Receives cargo from the ER, modifies it, and packages it into vesicles for delivery or secretion.
    - Fact: The Golgi apparatus modifies, sorts, packages, and distributes proteins and lipids into vesicles. [OpenStax, §4.4, 'The Golgi Apparatus' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/4-4-the-endomembrane-system-and-proteins)]
    - Fact: Golgi cisternae are flattened membranous sacs with a receiving cis face and an outgoing trans face. [OpenStax, §4.4, 'The Golgi Apparatus' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/4-4-the-endomembrane-system-and-proteins)]
  - **Mitochondrion** (mesh-to-structure mapping complete; meshes: mitochondrion-0..5 (6), mitochondrion-cristae-0..5 (6)): A double-membrane organelle with cristae that produces ATP by aerobic respiration. Function: Supplies most of the cell's ATP and participates in calcium and metabolic signalling.
    - Fact: Mitochondria produce ATP by aerobic respiration, and their inner membrane is folded into cristae. [OpenStax, §4.3, 'Mitochondria' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/4-3-eukaryotic-cells)]
    - Fact: Mitochondria contain their own DNA and ribosomes. [OpenStax, §4.3, 'Mitochondria' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/4-3-eukaryotic-cells)]
  - **Lysosome** (mesh-to-structure mapping complete; meshes: lysosome-0..6 (7), lysosome-core-0..6 (7)): An acidic, membrane-bound organelle containing hydrolytic enzymes. Function: Digests material taken in by endocytosis and recycles damaged cell components through autophagy.
    - Fact: Lysosomes contain hydrolytic enzymes that function at acidic pH and digest engulfed pathogens or worn-out organelles. [OpenStax, §4.3, 'Lysosomes' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/4-3-eukaryotic-cells)]
    - Fact: Compartmentalizing digestive enzymes inside lysosomes lets the cell break down material without harming the cytoplasm. [OpenStax, §3.4, 'Lysosomes' (https://openstax.org/books/microbiology/pages/3-4-unique-characteristics-of-eukaryotic-cells)]

### Muscle cell (Homo sapiens)

- **Domain / Cell type**: animal · Skeletal muscle fiber
- **Size & scale**: Diameter roughly 10–100 µm; length up to several centimetres — Schematic and unitless. Sarcomere spacing is widened for visibility; the model cannot be measured for real dimensions.
- **3D stats**: 81 mesh instances · ~24,736 estimated triangles · Capabilities: 3D procedural mesh, Structure camera focus, Cutaway shell toggle, Mesh-mapped highlighting, PNG screenshot export, GLB export capability · Preview: `/previews/muscle-cell.svg`
- **Summary**: A contractile syncytium: bundled myofibrils, repeating sarcomeres, T-tubules, calcium-storing sarcoplasmic reticulum, and peripheral nuclei.
- **Overview**: Skeletal muscle fibers are built for force. Each fiber contains bundles of myofibrils, and each myofibril is a chain of sarcomeres—the repeating units where actin and myosin filaments slide past one another. Excitation spreads deep into the fiber along T-tubules and triggers calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum. This schematic shows the architecture, not the molecular filament arrangement, and is not to scale along the fiber.
- **Traits**: Nucleus: Present; multiple, peripheral | Cell wall: Absent | Chloroplasts: Absent | Motility: Contractile (sarcomere shortening) | Typical size: 10–100 µm diameter; up to cm long | Organisation: Eukaryotic, multinucleated syncytium
- **Structures (7)**:
  - **Sarcolemma** (mesh-to-structure mapping complete; meshes: sarcolemma): The plasma membrane of a muscle fiber, capable of conducting an action potential. Function: Receives motor-neuron signals and propagates excitation along and into the fiber.
    - Fact: The sarcolemma is the plasma membrane surrounding a skeletal muscle fiber. [OpenStax, §10.2, 'Skeletal Muscle Fibers' (https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/10-2-skeletal-muscle)]
    - Fact: Action potentials sweep along the sarcolemma and are coupled to Ca2+ release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum. [OpenStax, §10.2, 'Excitation-Contraction Coupling' (https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/10-2-skeletal-muscle)]
  - **Myofibril** (mesh-to-structure mapping complete; meshes: myofibril-center, myofibril-inner, myofibril): A long bundle of actin and myosin filaments running the length of the muscle fiber. Function: Generates force through the coordinated shortening of its sarcomeres.
    - Fact: A muscle fiber contains many myofibrils made of repeating contractile units called sarcomeres. [OpenStax, §10.2, 'Skeletal Muscle Fibers' (https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/10-2-skeletal-muscle)]
    - Fact: The sequential arrangement of actin and myosin myofilaments gives skeletal muscle its striated appearance. [OpenStax, §10.2, 'Skeletal Muscle Fibers' (https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/10-2-skeletal-muscle)]
  - **Sarcomere** (mesh-to-structure mapping complete; meshes: sarcomere-z-0..6 (7), sarcomere-a-0..5 (6)): The repeating contractile unit between adjacent Z discs, containing actin and myosin filaments. Function: Shortens when myosin heads cycle along actin, pulling Z discs closer together.
    - Fact: A sarcomere is the functional contractile unit of a skeletal muscle fiber, extending between adjacent Z-discs. [OpenStax, §10.2, 'The Sarcomere' (https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/10-2-skeletal-muscle)]
    - Fact: During contraction, thin actin filaments are pulled and slide past thick myosin filaments as sarcomeres shorten. [OpenStax, §10.3, 'The Sliding Filament Model of Muscle Contraction' (https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/10-3-muscle-fiber-contraction-and-relaxation)]
  - **T-tubule** (mesh-to-structure mapping complete; meshes: t-tubule-ring-0..3 (4), t-tubule-cross-0..3 (4)): An invagination of the sarcolemma that carries excitation deep into the muscle fiber. Function: Brings the action potential close to the sarcoplasmic reticulum so calcium release is synchronised.
    - Fact: T-tubules carry action potentials into the interior of the muscle fiber to trigger Ca2+ release from the adjacent sarcoplasmic reticulum. [OpenStax, §10.2, 'Excitation-Contraction Coupling' (https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/10-2-skeletal-muscle)]
    - Fact: Two terminal cisternae of the sarcoplasmic reticulum and one T-tubule between them form a triad. [OpenStax, §10.2, 'Excitation-Contraction Coupling' (https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/10-2-skeletal-muscle)]
  - **Sarcoplasmic reticulum** (mesh-to-structure mapping complete; meshes: sr-cisterna-l-0..3 (4), sr-cisterna-r-0..3 (4), sarcoplasmic-reticulum): A specialised endoplasmic reticulum that stores and releases calcium ions. Function: Releases Ca²⁺ to trigger contraction and pumps it back to allow relaxation.
    - Fact: The sarcoplasmic reticulum stores Ca2+ and releases it when an action potential propagates along the T-tubules. [OpenStax, §10.2, 'Excitation-Contraction Coupling' (https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/10-2-skeletal-muscle)]
    - Fact: Active pumping of Ca2+ back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum allows tropomyosin to reshield actin-binding sites during relaxation. [OpenStax, §10.3, 'Muscle Fiber Contraction and Relaxation' (https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/10-3-muscle-fiber-contraction-and-relaxation)]
  - **Mitochondrion** (mesh-to-structure mapping complete; meshes: mitochondrion-0..7 (8), mitochondrion-cristae-0..7 (8)): An ATP-producing organelle packed between myofibrils in active muscle fibers. Function: Supplies ATP for contraction and for the calcium and ion pumps that restore the resting state.
    - Fact: Muscle tissue consumes large amounts of ATP because ATP is required for cross-bridge cycling and sustained contraction. [OpenStax, §3.2, 'Mitochondria' (https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/3-2-the-cytoplasm-and-cellular-organelles)]
    - Fact: Mitochondria produce ATP by aerobic respiration, and their inner membrane is folded into cristae. [OpenStax, §4.3, 'Mitochondria' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/4-3-eukaryotic-cells)]
  - **Nucleus** (mesh-to-structure mapping complete; meshes: nucleus-peripheral-0..3 (4), nucleolus-peripheral-0..3 (4)): One of many nuclei located at the periphery of a skeletal muscle fiber. Function: Directs protein synthesis for the large cytoplasmic volume of the fiber.
    - Fact: Skeletal muscle fibers are multinucleated, unlike cardiac and smooth muscle cells which typically contain a single nucleus. [OpenStax, §3.3, 'The Nucleus and DNA Replication' (https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/3-3-the-nucleus-and-dna-replication)]
    - Fact: Multiple nuclei provide multiple gene copies to produce large amounts of contractile proteins and enzymes. [OpenStax, §10.2, 'Skeletal Muscle Fibers' (https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/10-2-skeletal-muscle)]

### Red blood cell (Homo sapiens)

- **Domain / Cell type**: animal · Mature mammalian erythrocyte
- **Size & scale**: Roughly 7–8 µm diameter, ~2.5 µm thick at the rim — Schematic and unitless. Protein complexes and sugar chains are vastly enlarged relative to the cell disc so their spatial roles can be explored.
- **3D stats**: 140 mesh instances · ~21,592 estimated triangles · Capabilities: 3D procedural mesh, Structure camera focus, Cutaway shell toggle, Mesh-mapped highlighting, PNG screenshot export, GLB export capability · Preview: `/previews/red-blood-cell.svg`
- **Summary**: A flexible, anucleate biconcave disc packed with hemoglobin and supported by a sub-membrane spectrin skeleton for gas transport.
- **Overview**: Red blood cells are stripped down for oxygen and carbon dioxide transport. Lacking a nucleus and mitochondria leaves maximum space for hemoglobin while a biconcave geometry speeds gas diffusion and gives the cell deformability to squeeze through narrow capillaries. This schematic shows the membrane, underlying spectrin meshwork, hemoglobin matrix, ion exchangers, carbonic anhydrase, and surface glycocalyx at illustrative scales.
- **Traits**: Nucleus: Absent (enucleated when mature) | Cell wall: Absent | Chloroplasts: Absent | Motility: Passive (carried in blood flow) | Typical size: 7–8 µm | Organisation: Eukaryotic, specialised anucleate blood cell
- **Structures (6)**:
  - **Plasma membrane** (mesh-to-structure mapping complete; meshes: plasma-membrane): A flexible, biconcave phospholipid bilayer encapsulating the erythrocyte cytoplasm without rigid walls. Function: Maximises surface-area-to-volume ratio for gas diffusion and resists shear stress as the cell bends through capillaries.
    - Fact: Erythrocytes are biconcave discs, increasing their surface area-to-volume ratio for gas exchange and allowing them to fold through narrow capillaries. [OpenStax, §18.3, 'Erythrocytes' (https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/18-3-erythrocytes)]
    - Fact: Flexible structural proteins such as spectrin let erythrocytes deform as they pass through capillaries and spring back in wider vessels. [OpenStax, §18.3, 'Shape and Structure of Erythrocytes' (https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/18-3-erythrocytes)]
  - **Spectrin membrane skeleton** (mesh-to-structure mapping complete; meshes: spectrin-strut-0..59 (60), spectrin-node-0..9 (10)): A flexible sub-membrane filamentous network built from spectrin tetramers linked to short actin junctions. Function: Maintains the erythrocyte's biconcave shape and gives the membrane elastic reversibility after squeezing through microvessels.
    - Fact: A sub-membrane cytoskeleton of spectrin tetramers supports deformability and preserves the biconcave shape of human red blood cells. [Europe PMC / MDPI, §2, 'Structure of the Human Red Blood Cell Membrane' (https://europepmc.org/article/MED/28961212)]
    - Fact: Spectrin tetramers bind actin filaments and band 4.1 at junctional complexes and tether to band 3 via ankyrin. [Europe PMC / MDPI, §2, 'Structure of the Human Red Blood Cell Membrane' (https://europepmc.org/article/MED/28961212)]
  - **Hemoglobin cytoplasm** (mesh-to-structure mapping complete; meshes: hemoglobin-matrix, hemoglobin-tetramer-rim, hemoglobin-tetramer-inner): Dense, iron-rich tetrameric metalloproteins occupying nearly the entire interior of the mature erythrocyte. Function: Reversibly binds oxygen in the lungs and releases it to respiring tissues while buffering protons and assisting CO₂ transport.
    - Fact: As human erythrocytes mature they extrude their nucleus and most organelles, including mitochondria, leaving interior space for hemoglobin. [OpenStax, §18.3, 'Shape and Structure of Erythrocytes' (https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/18-3-erythrocytes)]
    - Fact: Each hemoglobin molecule contains four globin chains, each bound to an iron-containing heme group that can bind one oxygen molecule. [OpenStax, §18.3, 'Hemoglobin' (https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/18-3-erythrocytes)]
  - **Membrane transporters** (mesh-to-structure mapping complete; meshes: membrane-transporter-0..7 (8)): Abundant transmembrane protein channels, including Band 3 anion exchangers and aquaporin water pores. Function: Rapidly swap bicarbonate and chloride ions (the chloride shift) and equilibrate water across the membrane.
    - Fact: Band 3 is an abundant transmembrane glycoprotein (~25% of red cell membrane protein) that exchanges chloride and bicarbonate ions. [Europe PMC / MDPI, §3 & §6, 'Band 3' (https://europepmc.org/article/MED/28961212)]
    - Fact: Bicarbonate formed inside erythrocytes leaves into plasma in exchange for chloride ions (the chloride shift) during carbon dioxide transport. [OpenStax, §22.5, 'Bicarbonate Buffer' (https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/22-5-transport-of-gases)]
  - **Carbonic anhydrase** (mesh-to-structure mapping complete; meshes: carbonic-anhydrase): A cytosolic enzyme that catalyses the rapid interconversion of carbon dioxide and water with carbonic acid and bicarbonate. Function: Accelerates tissue CO₂ uptake into red blood cells and its conversion back to exhaled CO₂ in pulmonary capillaries.
    - Fact: Carbonic anhydrase inside erythrocytes catalyzes the conversion of carbon dioxide and water into carbonic acid, which dissociates into bicarbonate and hydrogen ions. [OpenStax, §22.5, 'Bicarbonate Buffer' (https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/22-5-transport-of-gases)]
  - **Surface glycocalyx** (mesh-to-structure mapping complete; meshes: glycocalyx-stalk-0..13 (14), glycocalyx-sugar-0..13 (14)): A negatively charged coat of glycoproteins and glycolipids extending from the outer leaflet of the plasma membrane. Function: Carries ABO and Rh blood-group antigens and creates electrostatic repulsion that prevents cells from clumping in vessels.
    - Fact: Erythrocyte membranes carry ABO blood-group antigens encoded as glycoproteins. [OpenStax, §18.6, 'ABO Blood Group' (https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/18-6-blood-typing)]
    - Fact: Carbohydrates bound to glycoproteins and glycolipids on the cell's exterior surface form the glycocalyx. [OpenStax, §5.1, 'Fluid Mosaic Model' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/5-1-components-and-structure)]

### Yeast cell (Saccharomyces cerevisiae)

- **Domain / Cell type**: fungi · Budding unicellular fungus
- **Size & scale**: Roughly 5–10 µm diameter — Schematic and unitless. Cell-wall layers, pore rings, and dispersed Golgi cisternae are scaled for clarity.
- **3D stats**: 70 mesh instances · ~20,072 estimated triangles · Capabilities: 3D procedural mesh, Structure camera focus, Cutaway shell toggle, Mesh-mapped highlighting, PNG screenshot export, GLB export capability · Preview: `/previews/yeast-cell.svg`
- **Summary**: A budding unicellular eukaryote with a chitin-glucan cell wall, chitinous bud scars, fungal vacuole, and polarised secretory growth into a daughter bud.
- **Overview**: Saccharomyces cerevisiae combines features familiar from other eukaryotes with distinctly fungal traits: a rigid wall rich in chitin and glucans rather than cellulose or peptidoglycan, a large vacuole that functions like a plant vacuole and animal lysosome, and asymmetric cell division by budding. This schematic captures a mother cell forming an emerging daughter bud along with chitin rings left by prior divisions.
- **Traits**: Nucleus: Present | Cell wall: Present (chitin and glucans) | Chloroplasts: Absent | Motility: Non-motile | Typical size: 5–10 µm | Organisation: Eukaryotic, unicellular fungus
- **Structures (7)**:
  - **Chitin–glucan cell wall** (mesh-to-structure mapping complete; meshes: cell-wall-mother, cell-wall-bud, bud-neck-ring, bud-scar-a, bud-scar-b): A tough polysaccharide wall made of glucans, mannoproteins, and chitin that encloses both mother cell and bud. Function: Resists osmotic lysis, maintains ovoid shape, and concentrates chitin in the bud-neck septum and persistent bud scars.
    - Fact: Fungal cell walls contain chitin and glucans—structural polysaccharides distinct from plant cellulose and bacterial peptidoglycan. [OpenStax, §24.1, 'Cell Structure and Function' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/24-1-characteristics-of-fungi)]
    - Fact: Somatic yeast cells divide asexually by budding, forming a daughter bulge on the side of the cell that detaches after nuclear division. [OpenStax, §24.1, 'Reproduction' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/24-1-characteristics-of-fungi)]
  - **Plasma membrane** (mesh-to-structure mapping complete; meshes: plasma-membrane-mother, plasma-membrane-bud): A phospholipid bilayer containing ergosterol beneath the fungal cell wall that regulates transport. Function: Mediates nutrient uptake, ion gradients, and exocytosis of new cell-wall components into the growing bud.
    - Fact: The plasma membrane is a phospholipid bilayer containing embedded proteins that lies inside the cell wall. [OpenStax, §4.3, 'The Plasma Membrane' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/4-3-eukaryotic-cells)]
    - Fact: Fungal plasma membranes are stabilized by ergosterol, a steroid molecule that replaces the cholesterol found in animal membranes. [OpenStax, §24.1, 'Cell Structure and Function' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/24-1-characteristics-of-fungi)]
  - **Nucleus** (mesh-to-structure mapping complete; meshes: nucleus, nucleus-chromatin, nucleolus, nuclear-pore): A double-membrane organelle housing yeast chromosomes inside a nuclear envelope that remains intact during mitosis. Function: Coordinates gene expression and migrates toward the bud neck prior to nuclear division.
    - Fact: Like other eukaryotes, yeast cells enclose DNA within a nuclear envelope punctuated with nuclear pores. [OpenStax, §4.3, 'The Nucleus' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/4-3-eukaryotic-cells)]
  - **Fungal vacuole** (mesh-to-structure mapping complete; meshes: vacuole-mother, vacuole-bud): An acidic membrane-bound compartment analogous to both lysosomes and plant vacuoles. Function: Stores amino acids and polyphosphate, maintains cytosolic pH, and degrades macromolecules via hydrolytic enzymes.
    - Fact: Vacuoles are membrane-bound eukaryotic compartments larger than vesicles that function in storage and transport. [OpenStax, §4.3, 'Vesicles and Vacuoles' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/4-3-eukaryotic-cells)]
  - **Mitochondrion** (mesh-to-structure mapping complete; meshes: mitochondrion-0..3 (4), mitochondrion-cristae-0..3 (4)): A dynamic cortical network of double-membrane organelles powering aerobic ATP production. Function: Generates ATP during oxidative respiration and partitions along actin cables into the emerging bud.
    - Fact: Mitochondria produce ATP by aerobic respiration using an inner membrane folded into cristae. [OpenStax, §4.3, 'Mitochondria' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/4-3-eukaryotic-cells)]
    - Fact: Yeasts are facultative anaerobes that grow best by aerobic respiration when oxygen is available and ferment when it is absent. [OpenStax, §24.1, 'Growth' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/24-1-characteristics-of-fungi)]
  - **Endoplasmic reticulum** (mesh-to-structure mapping complete; meshes: er-sheet-0..3 (4), er-ribosome): Ribosome-studded perinuclear and cortical membrane sheets continuous with the outer nuclear envelope. Function: Synthesises secretory proteins, cell-wall synthases, and membrane lipids needed for cell growth.
    - Fact: The endoplasmic reticulum is continuous with the nuclear envelope and collectively modifies proteins and synthesizes lipids. [OpenStax, §4.4, 'The Endoplasmic Reticulum' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/4-4-the-endomembrane-system-and-proteins)]
    - Fact: Membrane-bound ribosomes attached to the rough ER synthesize proteins destined for membranes or export from the cell. [OpenStax, §3.4, 'Ribosomes' (https://openstax.org/books/microbiology/pages/3-4-unique-characteristics-of-eukaryotic-cells)]
  - **Dispersed Golgi & vesicles** (mesh-to-structure mapping complete; meshes: golgi-cisterna-0..2 (3), golgi-secretory-vesicle): Unstacked Golgi cisternae distributed through the cytoplasm rather than clustered in one ribbon. Function: Sorts glycoproteins and aims secretory vesicles along actin cables into the expanding daughter bud.
    - Fact: The Golgi apparatus modifies, sorts, packages, and distributes proteins and lipids via transport vesicles. [OpenStax, §4.4, 'The Golgi Apparatus' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/4-4-the-endomembrane-system-and-proteins)]

### Paramecium (Paramecium caudatum)

- **Domain / Cell type**: protist · Freshwater ciliate protist
- **Size & scale**: Roughly 120–300 µm long — Schematic and unitless. Cilia rows are thinned from real densities and internal organelles are spaced so their roles stay legible.
- **3D stats**: 101 mesh instances · ~31,296 estimated triangles · Capabilities: 3D procedural mesh, Structure camera focus, Cutaway shell toggle, Mesh-mapped highlighting, PNG screenshot export, GLB export capability · Preview: `/previews/paramecium.svg`
- **Summary**: A ciliated unicellular protist with a flexible pellicle, oral feeding groove, dual macro- and micronucleus, and star-shaped contractile vacuoles.
- **Overview**: Paramecium caudatum is a complex single-celled eukaryote that carries out feeding, locomotion, osmotic water balance, and sexual exchange inside one cell. Rows of coordinated cilia propel the slipper-shaped cell through pond water while an oral groove sweeps bacteria into food vacuoles. Inside, star-shaped contractile vacuoles pump out incoming osmotic water, and two distinct nuclei divide genetic labor. Geometry is schematic and proportions are exaggerated for clarity.
- **Traits**: Nucleus: Present; dual (macro- and micronucleus) | Cell wall: Absent (flexible pellicle) | Chloroplasts: Absent | Motility: Ciliated swimming | Typical size: 120–300 µm | Organisation: Eukaryotic, unicellular ciliate protist
- **Structures (7)**:
  - **Pellicle** (mesh-to-structure mapping complete; meshes: pellicle-body, pellicle-posterior): A flexible yet supportive outer cortex formed by the plasma membrane backed by flattened alveolar sacs and cytoskeletal fibres. Function: Maintains the streamlined slipper contour while allowing elastic bending around obstacles.
    - Fact: Alveolate protists such as Paramecium possess membrane-enclosed sacs (alveoli) beneath the plasma membrane and a supportive outer pellicle. [OpenStax, §23.3, 'Alveolates: Dinoflagellates, Apicomplexans, and Ciliates' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/23-3-groups-of-protists)]
  - **Cilia** (mesh-to-structure mapping complete; meshes: cilium-0..59 (60)): Hundreds of short, hair-like microtubule-based organelles beating in coordinated waves across the pellicle. Function: Propel the cell along a helical path and reverse stroke direction quickly in avoiding reactions.
    - Fact: Paramecium swims using thousands of cilia driven by dynein motor ATPases sliding 9+2 axonemal microtubules in coordinated metachronal waves. [Europe PMC / MDPI, §2.5.1, 'Cilia and Calmodulin' (https://europepmc.org/article/MED/37110360)]
    - Fact: Cilia and eukaryotic flagella share an internal axoneme of nine outer microtubule doublets surrounding a central pair. [OpenStax, §4.5, 'Flagella and Cilia' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/4-5-the-cytoskeleton)]
  - **Oral groove & cytostome** (mesh-to-structure mapping complete; meshes: oral-groove-channel, oral-cytostome, oral-cytopharynx, oral-cilium-0..5 (6)): A ciliated ventral channel funneling suspended microbes inward toward the cell mouth (cytostome) and gullet. Function: Directs a feeding water current toward the cytostome, where particles are packaged into nascent food vacuoles.
    - Fact: Paramecium captures bacteria using cilia organized in an oral groove that acts as a primitive mouth. [OpenStax, §23.3, 'Alveolates: Dinoflagellates, Apicomplexans, and Ciliates' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/23-3-groups-of-protists)]
    - Fact: Cilia lining the gullet sweep microscopic prey into a food vacuole forming at the base of the gullet. [Europe PMC / MDPI, §1, 'Introduction' (https://europepmc.org/article/MED/37110360)]
  - **Macronucleus** (mesh-to-structure mapping complete; meshes: macronucleus-anterior, macronucleus-posterior, macronucleus-chromatin): A large, kidney-shaped polyploid nucleus containing numerous amplified copies of somatic genes. Function: Directs everyday transcription, metabolism, and vegetative growth across the large protist cell.
    - Fact: Ciliates carry a large polyploid macronucleus that serves as the site of transcription for metabolic and vegetative functions. [Europe PMC / MDPI, §2.3, 'Mating' (https://europepmc.org/article/MED/37110360)]
    - Fact: During vegetative cell division, the Paramecium macronucleus elongates and divides amitotically rather than by mitosis. [Europe PMC / MDPI, §1, 'Introduction' (https://europepmc.org/article/MED/37110360)]
  - **Micronucleus** (mesh-to-structure mapping complete; meshes: micronucleus): A small, diploid germline nucleus tucked close to the concave notch of the macronucleus. Function: Preserves the complete germline genome and exchanges haploid micronuclei during sexual conjugation.
    - Fact: Alongside the macronucleus, Paramecium carries one or more diploid micronuclei that divide by mitosis and preserve the germline genome. [Europe PMC / MDPI, §1 & §2.3 (https://europepmc.org/article/MED/37110360)]
    - Fact: During mating, complementary cells exchange haploid micronuclear products that fuse to form a diploid nucleus, while the old macronucleus disintegrates. [Europe PMC / MDPI, §2.3, 'Mating' (https://europepmc.org/article/MED/37110360)]
  - **Contractile vacuoles** (mesh-to-structure mapping complete; meshes: cv-bladder-0, cv-bladder-1, cv-canal-0-0..5 (6), cv-canal-1-0..5 (6)): Two star-shaped osmoregulatory organelles with radiating collecting canals at the anterior and posterior ends. Function: Continuously collect and pump excess water diffusing in from hypotonic pond water back outside the cell.
    - Fact: Freshwater Paramecium cells use two contractile vacuoles as osmoregulatory vesicles that fill with osmotic water and contract to expel it. [OpenStax, §23.3, 'Alveolates: Dinoflagellates, Apicomplexans, and Ciliates' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/23-3-groups-of-protists)]
  - **Food vacuoles** (mesh-to-structure mapping complete; meshes: food-vacuole-0..5 (6), food-vacuole-content-0..5 (6)): Membrane-bound digestive vesicles enclosing ingested microbes as they circulate through the cytoplasm. Function: Acidify, fuse with digestive enzymes, and deliver absorbed nutrients along cytoplasmic streaming (cyclosis) paths.
    - Fact: Waste particles are expelled when an exocytic vesicle fuses at a specific region on the Paramecium cell membrane called the anal pore. [OpenStax, §23.3, 'Alveolates: Dinoflagellates, Apicomplexans, and Ciliates' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/23-3-groups-of-protists)]

### Human brain (Homo sapiens)

- **Domain / Cell type**: animal · Central nervous system organ (intact 3D)
- **Size & scale**: Roughly 140 × 170 × 110 mm; ~1.3–1.4 kg — Schematic and unitless. Gyri, sulcal depths, and regional borders are stylised for clarity and cannot be used as clinical neuroimaging coordinates.
- **3D stats**: 25 mesh instances · ~32,000 estimated triangles · Capabilities: 3D procedural mesh, Structure camera focus, Cutaway shell toggle, Mesh-mapped highlighting, PNG screenshot export, GLB export capability · Preview: `/previews/human-brain.svg`
- **Summary**: An interactive whole-brain 3D model divided into functional cortical lobes, cerebellum, and brainstem, with a cutaway exposing the corpus callosum and limbic core.
- **Overview**: The human brain coordinates perception, voluntary movement, language, emotion, memory, and autonomic survival across specialised cortical lobes and subcortical hubs. Here, both cerebral hemispheres display folded gyri and sulci coloured by major anatomical and functional divisions—frontal, primary motor, primary somatosensory, parietal, temporal, and occipital—above the striated cerebellum and brainstem. Toggle Cutaway to remove the right cortical hemisphere and inspect the corpus callosum and deep limbic structures nestled inside.
- **Traits**: Anatomical system: Central nervous system | Protective coverings: Cranial cavity, meninges, and cerebrospinal fluid | Tissue composition: Cerebral cortex (gray matter), white-matter tracts, and subcortical nuclei | Primary functions: Sensory perception, motor control, homeostasis, language, emotion, and memory | Typical size: ~140 × 170 × 110 mm (~1.3–1.4 kg) | Organisation: Cerebrum, diencephalon, brain stem, and cerebellum
- **Structures (10)**:
  - **Frontal lobe** (mesh-to-structure mapping complete; meshes: frontal-lobe-right, frontal-lobe-left): The anterior cortical lobe governing executive planning, decision-making, working memory, and speech production. Function: Integrates prefrontal executive control, impulse inhibition, and anterior language circuits (such as Broca's area in the dominant hemisphere).
    - Fact: The frontal lobe sits anterior to the central sulcus and includes the prefrontal lobe responsible for personality, short-term memory, and consciousness. [OpenStax, §13.2, 'Cerebral Cortex' (https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/13-2-the-central-nervous-system)]
    - Fact: Neurons in the frontal lobe control cognitive functions including maintaining attention, speech, and decision-making. [OpenStax, §35.3, 'Brain: Cerebral Cortex' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/35-3-the-central-nervous-system)]
  - **Primary motor cortex** (mesh-to-structure mapping complete; meshes: motor-lobe-right, motor-lobe-left): The precentral gyrus immediately anterior to the central sulcus that initiates voluntary skeletal movements. Function: Maps contralateral body musculature somatotopically and projects upper motor neuron commands down the corticospinal tract.
    - Fact: The primary motor cortex occupies the precentral gyrus of the frontal lobe and directs upper motor neurons for voluntary movement. [OpenStax, §13.2, 'Cerebral Cortex' (https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/13-2-the-central-nervous-system)]
    - Fact: Each hemisphere's motor cortex controls muscles on the opposite side of the body via contralateral descending pathways. [OpenStax, §14.3, 'Descending Pathways' (https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/14-3-motor-responses)]
  - **Primary somatosensory cortex** (mesh-to-structure mapping complete; meshes: sensory-lobe-right, sensory-lobe-left): The postcentral gyrus immediately posterior to the central sulcus that receives touch, pressure, pain, and proprioceptive signals. Function: Maps tactile and proprioceptive inputs from contralateral body regions after relay through the thalamus.
    - Fact: The primary somatosensory cortex lies in the postcentral gyrus of the parietal lobe (Brodmann's areas 1, 2, and 3) and processes general tactile and proprioceptive sensations. [OpenStax, §13.2, 'Cerebral Cortex' (https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/13-2-the-central-nervous-system)]
    - Fact: The parietal lobe contains a somatosensory map of the body analogous to the motor map in the frontal lobe. [OpenStax, §35.3, 'Brain: Cerebral Cortex' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/35-3-the-central-nervous-system)]
  - **Parietal lobe** (mesh-to-structure mapping complete; meshes: parietal-lobe-right, parietal-lobe-left): The superior-posterior lobe behind the postcentral gyrus that integrates spatial awareness, multisensory perception, and reading. Function: Combines tactile, visual, and proprioceptive cues to construct body schema and spatial attention.
    - Fact: The parietal lobe sits posterior to the central sulcus and processes somatosensation, including touch, pressure, pain, and proprioception. [OpenStax, §13.2, 'Cerebral Cortex' (https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/13-2-the-central-nervous-system)]
  - **Temporal lobe** (mesh-to-structure mapping complete; meshes: temporal-lobe-right, temporal-lobe-left): The inferior lateral lobe beneath the lateral sulcus housing primary auditory cortex, speech comprehension, and memory interfaces. Function: Processes auditory signals, links spoken language in Wernicke's area, and connects closely with deep medial memory structures.
    - Fact: Separated inferiorly by the lateral sulcus, the temporal lobe processes primary auditory sensation and helps establish long-term memory. [OpenStax, §13.2, 'Cerebral Cortex' (https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/13-2-the-central-nervous-system)]
    - Fact: Medial temporal-lobe structures—the hippocampus and amygdala—are involved in long-term memory formation and emotional responses. [OpenStax, §13.2, 'Subcortical structures' (https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/13-2-the-central-nervous-system)]
  - **Occipital lobe** (mesh-to-structure mapping complete; meshes: occipital-lobe-right, occipital-lobe-left): The posterior cortical lobe above the cerebellum dedicated to primary visual reception and visual association. Function: Decodes retinotopic orientation, motion, colour, and spatial form delivered from the optic tracts via the thalamus.
    - Fact: The occipital lobe forms the posterior region of the cortex and contains Brodmann's areas 17 and 18 for primary visual perception. [OpenStax, §13.2, 'Cerebral Cortex' (https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/13-2-the-central-nervous-system)]
    - Fact: Complex visual information initiated in the occipital lobe is further processed across the temporal and parietal lobes. [OpenStax, §13.2, 'Cerebral Cortex' (https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/13-2-the-central-nervous-system)]
  - **Cerebellum** (mesh-to-structure mapping complete; meshes: cerebellum-right, cerebellum-left, cerebellum-vermis): The densely folded 'little brain' tucked beneath the occipital lobes posterior to the pons. Function: Compares motor plans with proprioceptive feedback to smooth posture, balance, timing, and coordinated movement.
    - Fact: The cerebellum coordinates movement and balance by comparing descending motor commands with sensory and proprioceptive feedback. [OpenStax, §13.2, 'The Cerebellum' (https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/13-2-the-central-nervous-system)]
    - Fact: The cerebellum accounts for approximately 10 percent of brain mass and has a folded surface covered in gyri and sulci. [OpenStax, §13.2, 'The Cerebellum' (https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/13-2-the-central-nervous-system)]
  - **Brainstem** (mesh-to-structure mapping complete; meshes: brainstem): The midline stalk comprising the midbrain, pons, and medulla oblongata linking forebrain and cerebellum to the spinal cord. Function: Routes ascending and descending nerve tracts while sustaining essential autonomic breathing, heart rate, and blood pressure reflexes.
    - Fact: The brain stem comprises the midbrain, pons, and medulla and regulates vital cardiovascular and respiratory functions. [OpenStax, §13.2, 'Brain Stem' (https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/13-2-the-central-nervous-system)]
    - Fact: Cranial nerves connect through the brain stem, and major ascending and descending pathways run through it between brain and spinal cord. [OpenStax, §13.2, 'Brain Stem' (https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/13-2-the-central-nervous-system)]
  - **Corpus callosum** (mesh-to-structure mapping complete; meshes: corpus-callosum): The thick C-shaped commissural tract of myelinated axons bridging the left and right cerebral hemispheres. Function: Allows continuous interhemispheric communication so both halves of the cortex share sensory, motor, and cognitive processing.
    - Fact: Deep within the cerebrum, the white matter of the corpus callosum provides the major pathway for communication between both cerebral hemispheres. [OpenStax, §13.2, 'The Cerebrum' (https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/13-2-the-central-nervous-system)]
    - Fact: The corpus callosum is a thick fiber bundle connecting the two hemispheres so information passes from one side to the other. [OpenStax, §35.3, 'Brain: Cerebral Cortex' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/35-3-the-central-nervous-system)]
  - **Deep limbic & thalamic core** (mesh-to-structure mapping complete; meshes: thalamus-right, thalamus-left, hippocampus-right, hippocampus-left, amygdala-right, amygdala-left, fornix-right, fornix-left): Subcortical relay and limbic structures (thalamus, hippocampus, amygdala, and fornix) enclosed beneath the cerebral cortex. Function: Relays sensory information to the cortex while driving emotional processing, threat appraisal, and long-term memory consolidation.
    - Fact: All sensory information except olfaction passes through the thalamus before cortical processing, while the limbic system links emotion, memory, and behavior. [OpenStax, §13.2, 'The Cerebrum' & 'Thalamus' (https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/13-2-the-central-nervous-system)]
    - Fact: Subcortical medial-lobe structures including the hippocampus and amygdala participate in long-term memory formation and emotional responses. [OpenStax, §13.2, 'Subcortical structures' (https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/13-2-the-central-nervous-system)]

### Human brain (cutout) (Homo sapiens)

- **Domain / Cell type**: animal · Sagittal & limbic neuroanatomy cutout
- **Size & scale**: Roughly 140 × 170 × 110 mm (open cutaway) — Schematic and unitless. Deep nuclei, ventricles, and cranial nerves are spaced slightly for visual separation and interactive picking rather than surgical precision.
- **3D stats**: 39 mesh instances · ~26,430 estimated triangles · Capabilities: 3D procedural mesh, Structure camera focus, Cutaway shell toggle, Mesh-mapped highlighting, PNG screenshot export, GLB export capability · Preview: `/previews/human-brain-cutout.svg`
- **Summary**: An open anatomical brain cutout exposing the limbic system (hippocampus, amygdala, cingulate gyrus, fornix), thalamus, hypothalamus, ventricles, and brainstem.
- **Overview**: Removing the right cortical shell reveals the tightly layered architecture beneath the cerebral cortex.
