Along the midline sit the corpus callosum, thalamus, hypothalamus, pituitary gland, ventricular cavities, brainstem, and cerebellum, framed by the C-shaped limbic system—cingulate gyrus, fornix, hippocampus, and amygdala—that links emotion, motivation, and long-term memory. Toggle Cutaway to hide the remaining left cortical hemisphere and view the subcortical organs in isolation.
- **Traits**: Anatomical system: Central nervous system | Protective coverings: Cranial meninges and ventricular cerebrospinal fluid | Tissue composition: Cerebral cortex, subcortical limbic nuclei, and white-matter commissures | Primary functions: Integrates sensory relay, homeostasis, emotion, and memory circuits | Typical size: ~140 × 170 × 110 mm (sagittal cutout) | Organisation: Mid-sagittal & subcortical CNS organ view
- **Structures (12)**:
  - **Cerebral cortex (cutaway hemisphere)** (mesh-to-structure mapping complete; meshes: cutout-left-hemisphere): The folded outer grey matter of the retained left cerebral hemisphere forming a sagittal shell around the deep brain. Function: Carries out conscious perception, language, reasoning, and voluntary motor planning across its gyri and sulci.
    - Fact: The cerebral cortex is a heavily folded sheet of gray matter with gyri (ridges) and sulci (grooves) enabling more gray matter to fit inside the skull. [OpenStax, §13.2, 'Cerebral Cortex' (https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/13-2-the-central-nervous-system)]
    - Fact: Beneath the cerebral cortex lie sets of subcortical nuclei and myelinated axons forming white matter. [OpenStax, §13.2, 'Subcortical structures' (https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/13-2-the-central-nervous-system)]
  - **Corpus callosum** (mesh-to-structure mapping complete; meshes: corpus-callosum): The broad C-shaped white-matter commissure (rostrum, genu, body, and splenium) bridging left and right hemispheres. Function: Transfers sensory, motor, and cognitive information rapidly across the cerebral midline.
    - Fact: The white matter of the corpus callosum provides the major pathway for communication between the left and right cerebral hemispheres. [OpenStax, §13.2, 'The Cerebrum' (https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/13-2-the-central-nervous-system)]
  - **Cingulate gyrus (limbic cortex)** (mesh-to-structure mapping complete; meshes: cingulate-gyrus-right, cingulate-gyrus-left): The arching cortical rim wrapping immediately dorsal to the corpus callosum along the medial hemisphere wall. Function: Integrates emotional appraisal, pain processing, conflict monitoring, and autonomic regulation within the limbic circuit.
    - Fact: The cingulate gyrus is part of the cerebral cortex located near the center of the brain inside the limbic system, regulating emotion, memory, and behavior. [OpenStax, §35.3, 'Limbic System' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/35-3-the-central-nervous-system)]
  - **Hippocampus** (mesh-to-structure mapping complete; meshes: hippocampus-right, hippocampus-left): A curved, seahorse-shaped medial temporal lobe structure central to forming new declarative memories. Function: Consolidates short-term experiences into long-term episodic and spatial memories before routing output via the fornix.
    - Fact: Located in the medial temporal lobe, the hippocampus is involved in long-term memory formation. [OpenStax, §13.2, 'Subcortical structures' (https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/13-2-the-central-nervous-system)]
  - **Amygdala** (mesh-to-structure mapping complete; meshes: amygdala-right, amygdala-left): Almond-shaped nuclear complexes sitting immediately anterior to the head of each hippocampus in the temporal lobe. Function: Evaluates emotional salience—especially fear, threat, and reward—and modulates autonomic arousal and emotional memory.
    - Fact: The amygdala is a temporal-lobe limbic structure involved in emotion, fear processing, and emotional responses. [OpenStax, §35.3, 'Limbic System' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/35-3-the-central-nervous-system)]
  - **Fornix & mammillary bodies** (mesh-to-structure mapping complete; meshes: fornix-right, fornix-left, mammillary-right, mammillary-left, anterior-commissure): An arched white-matter fibre bundle carrying hippocampal output beneath the corpus callosum down to the mammillary bodies. Function: Links the hippocampus with the hypothalamus and anterior thalamic nuclei as part of the Papez memory circuit.
    - Fact: The fornix arches from the hippocampus toward the mammillary bodies at the inferior-posterior hypothalamus as a limbic memory tract. [OpenStax, Unverified against local OpenStax extracts (originally Britannica 'Limbic system') (https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/13-2-the-central-nervous-system)]
    - Fact: The anterior thalamic nucleus relays signals between the hypothalamus and the emotion- and memory-producing limbic system. [OpenStax, §14.2, 'Diencephalon' (https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/14-2-central-processing)]
  - **Thalamus** (mesh-to-structure mapping complete; meshes: thalamus-right, thalamus-left, interthalamic-adhesion): Paired egg-shaped grey-matter relay hubs forming the dorsal diencephalon on either side of the third ventricle. Function: Filters, integrates, and relays ascending sensory and motor feedback signals to specific regions of the cerebral cortex.
    - Fact: All sensory information except the sense of smell passes through the thalamus before processing by the cerebral cortex. [OpenStax, §13.2, 'Thalamus' (https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/13-2-the-central-nervous-system)]
    - Fact: The thalami are paired ovoid masses flanking the walls of the third ventricle that make contact across the midline. [OpenStax, §13.2, 'The Diencephalon' (https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/13-2-the-central-nervous-system)]
  - **Hypothalamus & pituitary gland** (mesh-to-structure mapping complete; meshes: hypothalamus, infundibulum, pituitary-anterior, pituitary-posterior): The ventral diencephalic homeostatic regulator connected via the infundibulum stalk to the endocrine pituitary gland. Function: Maintains body temperature, hunger, thirst, circadian rhythms, autonomic balance, and neuroendocrine hormone release.
    - Fact: The hypothalamus lies inferior and anterior to the thalamus and regulates homeostasis, the autonomic nervous system, and the endocrine system via the pituitary gland. [OpenStax, §13.2, 'Hypothalamus' (https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/13-2-the-central-nervous-system)]
    - Fact: The pituitary gland is attached to the hypothalamus by the infundibulum (pituitary stalk) and stores or secretes hormones regulating body systems. [OpenStax, §17.3, 'The Pituitary Gland and Hypothalamus' (https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/17-3-the-pituitary-gland-and-hypothalamus)]
  - **Cerebral ventricles** (mesh-to-structure mapping complete; meshes: lateral-ventricle-right, lateral-ventricle-left, third-ventricle, cerebral-aqueduct, fourth-ventricle): The interconnected fluid-filled chambers (lateral, third, cerebral aqueduct, and fourth ventricles) containing cerebrospinal fluid. Function: Produce and circulate cerebrospinal fluid via choroid plexuses to buoy, cushion, and chemically bathe the central nervous system.
    - Fact: Four ventricles lined by ependymal cells and choroid plexus produce and circulate cerebrospinal fluid to cushion the CNS. [OpenStax, §13.3, 'Cerebrospinal Fluid' (https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/13-3-circulation-and-the-central-nervous-system)]
    - Fact: CSF flows from the lateral ventricles into the third ventricle, through the cerebral aqueduct, and into the fourth ventricle. [OpenStax, §13.3, 'Cerebrospinal Fluid Circulation' (https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/13-3-circulation-and-the-central-nervous-system)]
  - **Olfactory bulbs & optic nerves** (mesh-to-structure mapping complete; meshes: olfactory-tract-right, olfactory-tract-left, olfactory-bulb-right, olfactory-bulb-left, optic-chiasm, optic-nerve-right, optic-nerve-left, optic-tract-right, optic-tract-left): Anterior ventral sensory pathways: olfactory bulbs/tracts (CN I) beneath the frontal lobe and optic nerves/chiasm (CN II). Function: Convey smell directly to olfactory cortex and limbic centres, while routing visual input from the retinas through the optic chiasm.
    - Fact: Olfactory bulbs lie on the ventral surface of the frontal lobe, and olfaction reaches the cortex without passing through the thalamus. [OpenStax, §14.1, 'Olfaction' (https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/14-1-sensory-perception)]
    - Fact: Fibers of the optic nerve decussate at the optic chiasm and continue posteriorly as the optic tract toward the thalamus. [OpenStax, §14.2, 'Optic Chiasm' (https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/14-2-central-processing)]
  - **Cerebellum** (mesh-to-structure mapping complete; meshes: cerebellum-right, cerebellum-left, cerebellum-vermis): The striated hindbrain structure resting beneath the occipital cortex behind the fourth ventricle and pons. Function: Fine-tunes posture, balance, ocular tracking, and smooth motor execution through continuous sensory feedback.
    - Fact: Positioned posterior to the brain stem, the cerebellum compares motor commands from the cerebrum with proprioceptive feedback to coordinate movement. [OpenStax, §13.2, 'The Cerebellum' (https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/13-2-the-central-nervous-system)]
    - Fact: The cerebellum comprises roughly 10 percent of total brain mass and exhibits a folded surface of gyri and sulci. [OpenStax, §13.2, 'The Cerebellum' (https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/13-2-the-central-nervous-system)]
  - **Brainstem & spinal cord** (mesh-to-structure mapping complete; meshes: brainstem, spinal-cord): The continuous ventral-posterior neural axis of midbrain, pons, medulla oblongata, and upper cervical spinal cord. Function: Controls vital respiratory and cardiovascular rhythms while conducting ascending sensory and descending motor tracts.
    - Fact: The midbrain, pons, and medulla form the brain stem, bridging the forebrain and cerebellum with the spinal cord. [OpenStax, §13.1, 'Secondary Vesicles' (https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/13-1-the-embryologic-perspective)]
    - Fact: The pons and medulla regulate vital functions including cardiovascular and respiratory rates. [OpenStax, §13.2, 'Brain Stem' (https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/13-2-the-central-nervous-system)]
